blocks.html: Stephen Hawking (1942–2018) was a physicist at the University of Cambridge who studied black holes and the beginning of the universe. At 21 he was found to have motor neurone disease (ALS), which slowly paralyzed him; doctors expected him to live only a few years. He lived another 55, worked for most of them, and from 1985 spoke through a computer voice. From 1979 to 2009 he held the Lucasian chair of mathematics at Cambridge, the chair Isaac Newton once held.

A Brief History of Time (1988) explains, almost without equations, how physicists think about space and time, the expanding universe, black holes, and the search for one theory of everything. Hawking was told each equation would cut his sales, so he kept just one: Einstein's $E = mc^2$.

🏛️ Borrow the book

A Brief History of Time by Stephen Hawking is still under copyright, so we do not reproduce it. Find it at a library: Open Library or WorldCat. Look for the updated and expanded tenth anniversary edition (1998) or the illustrated edition (1996); they add a chapter on wormholes and time travel.

Hawking's best-known discovery, in 1974, was that black holes are not completely black: quantum effects near the edge should make them give off a faint glow, now called Hawking radiation, and very slowly shrink. It joined general relativity (the science of gravity) with quantum theory (the science of the very small) in one result. It has not yet been observed, because for real black holes the glow is far too faint. He wanted ordinary readers to share these ideas, and wrote a book for them.
Chapter titles are from the updated edition. Summaries are our own.

head: Chapter
What it is about, in our words
rows: 1. Our Picture of the Universe

How ideas about the universe changed from Aristotle and Ptolemy to Copernicus, Galileo and Newton, and what makes a good scientific theory: it explains what we see and makes predictions we can test.
Think about: Can a theory ever be proved right, or only not yet proved wrong?
2. Space and Time

Newton's absolute time gives way to Einstein: the speed of light is the same for everyone, and gravity is the bending of space and time by mass.
Think about: Why can't anything go faster than light?
3. The Expanding Universe

Galaxies are moving apart, as Hubble found in the 1920s; run the film backward and everything was once packed together, the big bang.
Think about: If the universe expands, what is it expanding into? (Hawking's answer: nothing; space itself stretches.)
4. The Uncertainty Principle

In quantum theory you cannot know both where a particle is and how fast it moves exactly; nature is a matter of chances.
Think about: How can something be in a definite place if we can't measure it exactly?
5. Elementary Particles and the Forces of Nature

Quarks, electrons and the four forces: gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak nuclear forces.
Think about: Why might physicists want the four forces to be one?
6. Black Holes

When a big star runs out of fuel it can collapse until not even light escapes. The edge is the event horizon.
Think about: Would you notice crossing an event horizon?
7. Black Holes Ain't So Black

Hawking's own discovery: black holes glow faintly and slowly evaporate.
Think about: Why is it so hard to test this one?
8. The Origin and Fate of the Universe

What the early universe was like, inflation, and Hawking's idea that the universe might have no edge or boundary in time.
Think about: Does a question like "what came before the big bang" have an answer?
9. The Arrow of Time

Why we remember the past but not the future: disorder (entropy) grows, and the universe's expansion points the same way.
Think about: Why can't a broken cup put itself back together?
10. Wormholes and Time Travel

Whether shortcuts through space or trips to the past are allowed by physics (added in later editions).
Think about: What is the grandfather paradox?
11. The Unification of Physics

Attempts to join gravity with quantum theory, including string theory.
Think about: Is a theory of everything the end of physics?
Conclusion

Why people ask why the universe exists, and why science and philosophy both matter to that question.
Think about: What would knowing the final theory change for you?
blocks.cap: A Brief History of Time: a reading guide (updated edition).

blocks.html: Light travels about 300,000 km each second. The Sun is about 150 million km away, so its light takes about 500 seconds, a little over 8 minutes, to reach us. When you look at the Sun, you see it as it was 8 minutes ago. Look far enough and you see the young universe.

blocks.title: Light from the Sun
blocks.q: Light goes 300,000 km per second. The Sun is 150,000,000 km away. How many seconds does sunlight take to reach Earth?

blocks.title: How big is a black hole?
blocks.q: The event horizon of a black hole is about 3 km in radius for each Sun's worth of mass. What is the radius for a black hole of 10 solar masses?
blocks.a: About 30 km: a city-sized object with ten times the Sun's mass.

blocks.html: Thinking a black hole sucks in everything around it like a drain. Far away, its gravity is the same as any star of the same mass. If the Sun turned into a black hole of the same mass, Earth would keep the same orbit (though it would get very cold).

blocks.html: The Universe in a Nutshell (2001) was Hawking's follow-up, written for readers who found the first book hard. It is shorter, full of color pictures, and each chapter can be read on its own after the first two. The title comes from a line in Shakespeare's Hamlet: "I could be bounded in a nutshell, and count myself a king of infinite space."

The book covers relativity, the shape of time, how the universe began, whether we can predict the future, whether time travel is possible, and newer ideas such as branes. Hawking says plainly which ideas are well tested and which are guesses.

🏛️ Borrow the book

The Universe in a Nutshell by Stephen Hawking is still under copyright, so we do not reproduce it. Find it at a library: Open Library or WorldCat.

head: Chapter
What it is about, in our words
rows: 1. A Brief History of Relativity

How Einstein came to special and general relativity, and why light's speed being the same for everyone changes how time and space behave.
Tested or speculative: Well tested
2. The Shape of Time

Time as a dimension that can be bent, and "imaginary time," a mathematical tool Hawking used to describe the beginning of the universe.
Tested or speculative: Relativity: tested. Imaginary time: a mathematical idea
3. The Universe in a Nutshell

How the whole universe might have grown from something tiny, with inflation and quantum effects.
Tested or speculative: Partly tested (the big bang); partly speculative
4. Predicting the Future

Why the future is hard to predict exactly: chaos, quantum uncertainty, and what black holes do to information.
Tested or speculative: Mixed
5. Protecting the Past

Whether the laws of physics allow travel to the past, and Hawking's "chronology protection" idea that they may prevent it.
Tested or speculative: Speculative
6. Our Future? Star Trek or Not?

How fast knowledge, technology and people themselves might change in coming centuries.
Tested or speculative: Hawking's own forecasts
7. Brane New World

The idea that our universe might be a surface (a brane) in a space with more dimensions.
Tested or speculative: Speculative; not tested

blocks.text: How to read a science book like this

items: Keep a note of three kinds of claims: things measured and tested, things predicted but not yet tested, and the author's guesses.
Look at the pictures before the text; this book was designed around them.
Read chapters 1 and 2 first, then any order.
When you meet a big number, write it in powers of ten and compare it to something you know.

blocks.title: Time slows down
blocks.q: In relativity, a clock moving at 87% of light speed ticks at half the rate of one at rest. If 10 years pass on Earth, how much time passes for a traveler at that speed?
blocks.a: 5 years. This slowing has been measured with fast particles and with atomic clocks flown on airplanes.

blocks.html: Treating every idea in the book as proven. Hawking himself labels some as speculation. Relativity is tested; branes and time travel are not.
Read more: The Universe in a Nutshell.

blocks.html: Carl Sagan (1934–1996) was an astronomer at Cornell University who worked on NASA's missions to the planets, including the Viking landers on Mars and the Voyager probes, for which he helped make the Golden Record carrying sounds and pictures from Earth. He was also one of the best-known science explainers of his time. His television series Cosmos: A Personal Voyage (1980) was watched by hundreds of millions of people, and the book Cosmos came out the same year.

Cosmos tells the history of science and the story of the universe together: how people learned the size of the Earth, the motions of planets, the lives of stars and the evolution of life, and what that means for us. Its thirteen chapters follow the thirteen episodes.

🏛️ Borrow the book

Cosmos by Carl Sagan is still under copyright, so we do not reproduce it. Find it at a library: Open Library or WorldCat.

Sagan's most famous teaching tool squeezes the whole history of the universe into one calendar year. The big bang is the first moment of January 1; now is midnight at the end of December 31. Sagan used the best age known at the time; we use about 13.8 billion years.

blocks.name: iv-calendar
blocks.cap: Pick an event and see where it falls on the Cosmic Calendar. One day stands for about 38 million years, one second for about 440 years.

blocks.title: Calendar math
blocks.q: If the universe is 13.8 billion years old and that is squeezed into 365 days, how many years does one calendar day stand for?

blocks.title: The dinosaurs
blocks.q: The dinosaurs (other than birds) died out about 66 million years ago. How many calendar days before midnight on December 31 is that?
steps: One day is about 37.8 million years.

head: Chapter
What it is about, in our words
rows: 1. The Shores of the Cosmic Ocean
A tour of the universe from galaxies to Earth, and Eratosthenes measuring the Earth with shadows and a stick, around 240 BC.
2. One Voice in the Cosmic Fugue
Evolution and the chemistry of life; how all living things are related.
3. The Harmony of Worlds
Astrology versus astronomy, and Johannes Kepler's long struggle to find the true shapes of planetary orbits.
4. Heaven and Hell
Comets, impacts and the scorching greenhouse of Venus.
5. Blues for a Red Planet
Mars in story and in science, and what the Viking landers found.
6. Travelers' Tales
The Voyager probes and the age of Dutch explorers and scientists like Christiaan Huygens.
7. The Backbone of Night
What the stars are, and how the early Greek thinkers of Ionia began asking natural questions.
8. Travels in Space and Time
Light speed, relativity, and what travel to the stars would mean.
9. The Lives of the Stars
How stars are born, shine and die, and how they made the atoms in us.
10. The Edge of Forever
Galaxies, the expanding universe and the big bang.
11. The Persistence of Memory
Genes, brains, books and how information is stored.
12. Encyclopaedia Galactica
The search for life beyond Earth and how we might talk to it.
13. Who Speaks for Earth?
The Library of Alexandria, the cost of losing knowledge, and humanity's future.

blocks.html: Cosmos has a few passages where Sagan states his own views on history, religion and politics. Read them as one scientist's opinions, and compare other views. The science chapters have aged well, though some numbers (such as the age of the universe) have been updated since 1980.
Thinking the Cosmic Calendar is a real calendar. It is a scale model in time, like a map is a scale model in space.

blocks.html: Sagan wrote or co-wrote about twenty books. Here are the best known, what each is about in our own words, and why it is worth reading. All are still under copyright, so look for them at a library.
Across his books, Sagan's big theme is how to know what is true: look for evidence, test claims, and be willing to change your mind, while keeping a sense of wonder.

head: Book
Year
What it is about
rows: The Cosmic Connection
Short essays on the planets, life in the universe and our place in it.
The Dragons of Eden
How the human brain and intelligence evolved; it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1978 and introduced the Cosmic Calendar.
Broca's Brain
Essays on science, scientists and claims at the edge of science.
Cosmos
The book of the television series (see the previous topic).
Contact
A novel about a scientist who receives a message from the stars; made into a film in 1997.
Pale Blue Dot
Our future in space, named for the 1990 Voyager photo in which Earth is a tiny speck.
The Demon-Haunted World
How to think clearly about claims, written with help from Ann Druyan; it includes his "baloney detection kit" of thinking tools.
Billions and Billions
His last essays, published after his death.

🏛️ Borrow the book

The Demon-Haunted World by Carl Sagan is still under copyright, so we do not reproduce it. Find it at a library: Open Library or WorldCat. Also search for Pale Blue Dot and The Dragons of Eden.

blocks.text: Thinking tools, in our own words

blocks.html: In The Demon-Haunted World Sagan collects tools for checking a claim. Here are some of them, restated:

items: Look for independent confirmation of the facts.
Encourage debate among people who know the evidence.
Don't trust a claim just because an important person makes it.
Think of more than one explanation, and test each.
Measure if you can: numbers help you tell explanations apart.
Every link in a chain of argument must hold.
Prefer the simpler explanation when two fit the facts equally well.
Ask whether the claim could, in principle, be shown false.

blocks.html: He also made famous a short rule: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. A surprising claim needs strong evidence before we accept it.

blocks.title: The pale blue dot
blocks.q: When Voyager 1 photographed Earth in 1990 it was about 6 billion km away. Light goes about 300,000 km per second. About how many hours did the light from Earth take to reach the probe?

blocks.html: Thinking skepticism means rejecting new ideas. Sagan meant asking for evidence, and accepting a new idea when the evidence is good. He supported the search for life beyond Earth while asking for proof of every claim.
Read more: Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot and The Demon-Haunted World.
